title: The saw, alone
tomorrow: two extremes, one middle. what did he tell his five old friends?

segments.voice: Yesterday, MN 118: sixteen steps, starting with simply knowing a long breath as long. Today, a sutta for when someone's words land like a blade.
screen: `SIXTEEN STEPS.` → `WHEN WORDS LAND LIKE A BLADE.`

segments.voice: Press your palm flat against the floor for a second. Solid. It doesn't flinch when someone walks on it, or drops a bag, or spills a drink. Now the opposite: a comment under your post, a remark in class, and suddenly your whole chest is a fist. MN 21, read straight through, answers with that floor. Someone takes a hoe and a basket and says, i'll make this great earth not be earth. He digs and scatters and digs. Can he do it?
screen: `PALM FLAT ON THE FLOOR.` → `A COMMENT, AND YOUR CHEST IS A FIST.` → `A HOE AGAINST THE WHOLE EARTH.`

segments.voice: No, the sutta says. The earth is deep and vast; he'll only wear himself out. Then the Buddha turns it toward speech. People will talk to you in five ways, he says, in paraphrase: at the right time or the wrong time, truly or falsely, gently or harshly, to help or to harm, with goodwill or with hate. Whatever they choose, train like this: my mind stays unshaken, no harsh word comes out of me, i keep goodwill toward them, and i fill the world with a mind like the earth, wide, without hostility. Then more pictures, all physical. Try to paint pictures on empty space with dye: nothing sticks. Try to burn a great river with a grass torch: it won't catch. Stroke a soft, tanned catskin bag with your hand: it doesn't crackle. And the sutta's name comes from its hardest image, which younger listeners can skip past: even if bandits cut you with a saw, a mind that turns to hate isn't following the teaching. The point isn't to stay where you're hurt. It's that their words don't get to decide what your mind becomes.
screen: `THE EARTH IS TOO DEEP TO DIG AWAY.` · `FIVE WAYS PEOPLE SPEAK TO YOU.` · `PAINT ON SPACE. BURN A RIVER.` · `THE SAW: HATE ISN'T THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `A MIND LIKE THE EARTH.`

segments.voice: Put both palms on the floor or the ground beside you, and keep them there the whole sit. Feel how it holds your weight without pushing back. Bring to mind one sharp thing someone said, let it land, and feel the ground under your hands stay just as it is. If you can, end by wishing that person well, once.
The saw: MN 21, the simile of the saw, on keeping goodwill even when words, or worse, come at you.
A mind like the earth: dig all you like, it stays earth. Sutta three, read alone.

screen: `DAY 1705 COUNTS.` → `THE PALI SOURCES, ALONE · 3 OF 12.` → `TOMORROW: TWO EXTREMES, ONE MIDDLE. WHAT DID HE TELL THEM?`

howItsDone: The simile of the saw is taught in Buddhist communities as a standard for patience (khanti) and goodwill; some practitioners recall the earth simile when they're criticized.

original.note: Pali: saw. MN 21 is the Kakacupama Sutta, the simile of the saw.

MN 21.meaning: the Kakacupama Sutta, the simile of the saw

MN 118.meaning: the sutta on mindfulness of breathing

goodwill.meaning: metta: wishing someone well, even someone who hurt you

sutta.meaning: a discourse of the Buddha, in Pali

notes: MN 21 paraphrased: the five courses of speech (timely/untimely, true/untrue, gentle/harsh, beneficial/unbeneficial, with goodwill/with inner hate); the training ('our minds will be unaffected, we shall utter no evil words, we shall abide compassionate... pervading the all-encompassing world with a mind similar to the earth'); the similes of earth and hoe, painting on space, burning the Ganges with a grass torch, the catskin bag; the saw. Confirm order (in the sutta the earth simile follows the five courses).
The opening Vedehika story (the mistress whose gentleness fails under her maid Kali's test) is left out for length.
For parents: the saw image is mentioned once, without detail, with a 'younger listeners can skip past' line.

'The point isn't to stay where you're hurt' and the myth reveal are interpretive (the sutta addresses inner state and speech, not whether to remain in harm). Keeper to confirm the phrasing is fair to the text.
Gloss 'goodwill' gives metta as the Pali; the sutta's word in the training is metta (mettacitta). Confirm.
